## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

17	// behavior-defining is read by the session from the tracked task files at HEAD;
18	// the prompt says which issue and which nonce, and the session validates both in
19	// code before acting (DESIGN §7).
20	
21	export const DEFAULT_ENDPOINT = 'default';
22	
23	// The endpoint is a ROUTINE'S API TRIGGER — `POST /v1/claude_code/routines/
24	// <trigger-id>/fire` with a per-routine bearer token — which is what Claude Code
25	// on the web actually exposes to an HTTP caller. Three consequences the design's
26	// "a CCR API call" did not spell out, each verified against the routines docs
27	// rather than assumed:
28	//
29	//  - THE BEHAVIOR IS THE ROUTINE'S STORED PROMPT, not ours. `text` reaches the
30	//    session wrapped in a `<routine-fire-payload>` block explicitly labelled
31	//    untrusted, and a routine acts on it only because its own saved prompt says
32	//    to. That is the issue-is-data posture arriving for free at one more hop: our
33	//    payload names an item, and every instruction comes from a stored artifact.
34	//    The routine's stored prompt is one line pointing at `instructions.md` beside
35	//    this file, so the whole of what a session does is tracked and reviewed.
36	//  - THE BODY CARRIES ONE FIELD. `text` is freeform and unparsed — structured
37	//    JSON would arrive as a literal string — so the item number and nonce go in
38	//    as prose, and nothing else goes in at all.
39	//  - THERE IS NO IDEMPOTENCY KEY (standing entry 11, answered: the endpoint
40	//    offers none), which is exactly why THIS MODULE CALLS ONCE PER ITEM AND NEVER
41	//    RETRIES. A retry is only safe when you know the first call did nothing, and
42	//    a client-side timeout is the one case where you cannot know — the session
43	//    may well have started. Retrying there is what would make invocation
44	//    at-least-once and put two sessions on one item; declining to retry is what
45	//    keeps it at-most-once and lets the whole agent-side claim protocol delete.
46	//    An outcome we did not learn is reported as UNKNOWN and resolved by the agent
47	//    leash, which is a rule that already exists, rather than by a guess here.
48	//
49	// The beta header is dated and the endpoint is a research preview whose two most
50	// recent header versions keep working, so it lives in config with a default here
51	// — a rotation is then a config edit on one repo, never an engine release the
52	// whole fleet waits for.
53	export const DEFAULT_HEADERS = Object.freeze({
54	  'anthropic-beta': 'experimental-cc-routine-2026-04-01',
55	  'anthropic-version': '2023-06-01',
56	});
57	
58	// The endpoint a task's hand-off calls, resolved against the repo's config.
59	// Returns `{ name, url, tokenEnv, headers }` or `{ name, error }` — a task naming
60	// an endpoint the repo has not configured is a repo-configuration fact, reported
61	// where the operator reads it, never a crash.
62	export function resolveEndpoint(config, task) {
63	  const name = task?.decl?.invocation_endpoint ?? DEFAULT_ENDPOINT;
64	  const endpoints = config?.taskScheduler?.endpoints ?? {};
65	  const entry = endpoints[name];
66	  if (!entry) {
67	    return { name, error: `this repo's config declares no invocation endpoint "${name}" (taskScheduler.endpoints)` };
68	  }
69	  if (!entry.url) return { name, error: `invocation endpoint "${name}" declares no url` };
70	  if (!entry.tokenSecret) return { name, error: `invocation endpoint "${name}" declares no tokenSecret (the NAME of the repo Actions secret holding its token)` };
71	  return { name, url: entry.url, tokenEnv: entry.tokenSecret, headers: { ...DEFAULT_HEADERS, ...(entry.headers ?? {}) } };
72	}
73	
74	// The fire payload: which item, and the nonce that proves this call is the one
75	// the hand-off comment recorded. Prose, not JSON — the field is freeform and
76	// unparsed, so a structured payload would arrive as a literal string — and
77	// deliberately free of instructions, because the routine's stored prompt is what
78	// says how to act on it (see `instructions.md`). The session still validates
79	// the item in code before touching it: a payload labelled untrusted is trusted no
80	// more than a label event was.
81	export const firePayload = ({ repo, item, nonce }) =>
82	  `Claudinite work item: ${repo}#${item.number}. Invocation nonce: ${nonce}.`;
83	
84	// The invoker seam the executor calls, exactly once per item. Failure is DATA,
85	// never a throw, and it comes in two kinds the caller must treat differently:
86	//
87	//   { ok: true, sessionId, sessionUrl }   the routine fired; a session exists
88	//   { ok: false, answered: true, error }  the endpoint ANSWERED and refused —
89	//                                         no session, and the cause is a
90	//                                         configuration fault a retry cannot fix
91	//   { ok: false, answered: false, error } no answer reached us — a timeout, a
92	//                                         dropped connection. The session may or
93	//                                         may not exist, and nothing here may
94	//                                         guess which.
95	export function agentInvoker({ repo, config, env = process.env, fetchImpl = fetch, timeoutMs = 60e3 }) {
96	  return async function invoke({ task, item, nonce }) {
97	    const endpoint = resolveEndpoint(config, task);
98	    // A configuration fault, decided before any call: definite, and no session.
99	    if (endpoint.error) return { ok: false, answered: true, error: endpoint.error };
100	    const token = env[endpoint.tokenEnv];
101	    if (!token) {
102	      // The `required_secrets` posture, applied to the endpoint token: nothing
103	      // fails silently, the task just doesn't work yet, and the item names which
104	      // secret to set (DESIGN §14.7).
105	      return { ok: false, answered: true, error: `the Actions secret \`${endpoint.tokenEnv}\` for invocation endpoint "${endpoint.name}" is not set in this repo` };
106	    }
107	
108	    const payload = { text: firePayload({ repo, item, nonce }) };
109	
110	    // ONE call. No loop, and deliberately no `attempts` knob for anyone to raise.
111	    try {
112	      const res = await fetchImpl(endpoint.url, {
113	        method: 'POST',
114	        headers: {
115	          ...endpoint.headers,
116	          'content-type': 'application/json',
117	          authorization: `Bearer ${token}`,
118	          'user-agent': 'claudinite-executor',
119	        },
120	        body: JSON.stringify(payload),
121	        signal: AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs),
122	      });
123	      let json = null;
124	      try { json = await res.json(); } catch { json = null; }
125	      if (res.status >= 200 && res.status < 300) {
126	        return {
127	          ok: true,
128	          sessionId: json?.claude_code_session_id ?? null,
129	          sessionUrl: json?.claude_code_session_url ?? null,
130	        };
131	      }
132	      // A status came back, so the endpoint decided: no session was started, and
133	      // the cause is a token, a URL or a routine — none of which a retry fixes.
134	      return {
135	        ok: false, answered: true,
136	        error: `endpoint "${endpoint.name}" returned ${res.status}${json?.error ? `: ${JSON.stringify(json.error)}` : ''}`,
137	      };
138	    } catch (e) {
139	      // Nothing came back. The request may have landed and started a session, so
140	      // this is the one outcome that must never be retried and never be reported
141	      // as a failure — it is genuinely unknown, and the caller says so on the item.
142	      return { ok: false, answered: false, error: `endpoint "${endpoint.name}" gave no answer: ${e.message}` };
143	    }
144	  };
145	}

107	   Advisory there is *diagnostic*: it names the cause the moment it appears.
108	   - **Prefer a positive allowlist over an enumerated list of the bad cases.** Match the one allowed

110	     catches a variant that doesn't exist yet the day it lands, and turns an indirection (a value

[engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md): **does it constrain a *static
signature in the repo artifact* — something a post-hoc scan could observe?**

- **Yes → a conversion candidate.** A dangling-reference rule, a filename convention, a workflow
  or manifest shape, a "these two files must agree" invariant, a forbidden pattern in code.
- **No → leave it.** In-flight process (leaves no artifact — "see the test fail first"),
  judgment ("name by scope"), or knowledge whose failure is only visible at runtime (jsdom
  diverging from Chrome). These are why the rule is prose; don't force them.

**"Already covered by another check" is a claim to test, not to reason out** — hand the sibling check a file
that violates the rule before dropping the candidate as a duplicate. A ban list only covers the routes whoever
wrote it thought of, so the routes it misses are invisible to exactly the reasoning that drew it: three sweeps
running dropped an "the app opens no socket" rule because a neighbouring check banned the obvious networking
import, while the base library re-exported a raw socket call that sailed straight through.

**"Not statically checkable" is a verdict about the tree's shape when it was taken, not about the rule —
re-derive it against today's sources.** A removal, a migration or a consolidation can collapse the entry points
a rule had to cover, and the objection dies with them: a "one deletable storage directory" rule needed
data-flow tracing while many entry points wrote paths, and needed none once one root remained. So when a sweep
meets prose an earlier sweep left behind, re-ask the question rather than trusting the recorded answer. (This
covers the *technical* verdict only — an owner's rejection of a conversion is settled.)

**Read the conversion tracker's prior comments before authoring, not after.** Independent re-derivation is
exactly how duplicate work happens: a fresh reading of the same prose will happily re-nominate a rule, build it
out in full, and only then discover it was built and rejected before. The tracker is a precondition of the
work, not a place to log it — and record each rejection with its reason so the next run can act on it.

**A static signature is necessary, not sufficient.** Both shapes the working-discipline rules bar
— a rule that pins today's code in place, and one derivable from the product's requirements —
answer *yes* here, so screen every candidate against that bar before converting it. Leave either
where it is; routing a requirement to the spec and its suite is its own change, not this sweep's.

The check-the-world rule from DESIGN holds: if a rule is always-testable, it was never really
part of the on-demand skill — it belongs in a pack as a check.

## How to convert one

Follow the extract stage's check-authoring discipline (the local promotion ladder in
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). For each candidate:

> **The upgrade-pass caller lands inside growth-extract's own PR**, which auto-merges after CI — so the
> see-it-fail fixture is the only gate a converted check gets there. Convert only what you can prove;
> anything shakier stays prose and waits for the weekly sweep's reviewed PR.

1. **Author the check** in the owning pack (`<pack>/<rule>.mjs`, listed in its `pack.mjs`) — the
   failure message *is* the rule (what / why / fix / `doc:` pointer back to the prose).
2. **Write the fixture first and see it fail** — a violating fixture must find, a clean one must
   not (the test lives beside the pack's other tests). A conversion with no proving fixture
   doesn't ship.
3. **Ship at real severity, fail-fast** — blocking for a defect, advisory when the rule is
   directional by kind, or when the condition is blocking-grade but **irreversible by the time it is
   observable** (an append-only transcript, a published artifact). A blocking finding no edit can
   retract never converges — it spends every remaining Stop cycle on something nothing can fix.
   Advisory there is *diagnostic*: it names the cause the moment it appears.
   - **Prefer a positive allowlist over an enumerated list of the bad cases.** Match the one allowed
     shape and flag everything else, rather than banning the violations you can name. An allowlist
     catches a variant that doesn't exist yet the day it lands, and turns an indirection (a value
     passed through a variable instead of written literally) into a finding too — refusing to reason
     about indirection is the feature. Invert only where the allowed set is genuinely open-ended.
4. **Delete the prose the check now covers** — whole, never trimmed. The deletion test below is
   how you decide which paragraphs those are.

**Before writing a rule off as un-checkable, try parsing the file's structure instead of grepping
its text.** Grep finds the pattern anywhere; parsing finds it in the one spot the rule means —
which kills the false alarm. (Example: `Authorization` is only wrong inside a CloudFront policy's
*own* header list, not elsewhere in the template.) Parse only as much as you need, and hold the
check to the same fixture bar.

**When a rule mandates a *form*, the check asserts that form — never the intent behind it.** Where
the prose says *write it exactly like this*, the check's whole job is deciding whether the artifact
is that form; inferring what the author meant is unbounded in the wrong direction and leaves the
likeliest reproduction uncaught, since a hand-picked marker list always misses the phrasing nobody
enumerated. Expect a form check to fire on something that breaks the form while causing no harm —
that's the rule as written doing its job, not a reason to re-add intent-guessing.

When even a scoped parser can't make detection confident, **leave the prose and log the
candidate** to a tagged conversion-backlog issue rather than shipping a shaky check.

## Coming out: the deletion test

Coming out of a conversion, apply the **deletion test**: prose a mechanism fully covers is
deleted, never trimmed. Ask it of every paragraph standing beside a landed check — *with this
paragraph gone, would the check still catch every violation it describes **and** tell the agent
how to fix it?* If yes, it is redundant: delete it whole. The check's failure message is where
the rule lives now and its header comment is where the rationale lives, so a paragraph restating
either pays twice and is the drift trap waiting to spring.

Before concluding prose is the only carrier, look at the pack's **skills** too — an
activity-scoped skill often already holds the map a rule is repeating. Keep only what no artifact
carries.

The test **discriminates** rather than just deleting: a paragraph stays whole whenever it carries
something the check does not — a second rule in the same breath, an exemption the check can't
encode, a value the check can't judge, or a remedy the finding's own `fix` line never states
(a finding renders `what` / `why` / `fix` / `doc`, never the rule's `description`, so a remedy
that lives only in the description is not carried). Two worked calls: an `npm test` invariant
went entirely — the check caught it and the testing-guide skill already listed the suites —
while an `extension-test/` mirror bullet stayed, because the check beside it enforced only the
`package.json` list's sync with the tree and never the mirror convention itself.

Whether a check covers a rule is a judgment about meaning, so this test is applied by a
**reader**, not mechanized.

## Bounds

- **One PR, bounded surface** — the new rule module, its `pack.mjs` line, its fixture, and the
  trimmed prose. Don't "improve" unrelated rules while you're in there.
- **Never delete a rule you didn't convert** — the deletion test is only ever asked of a rule a
  *landed* check now enforces.
- Run the suite and the sweep green before the PR goes up, and never push to `main` directly. The
  sweep opens its own PR for the owner's approval; the upgrade pass adds its conversion to the
  growth-extract PR already being opened, and opens none of its own.

### The dedupe claim three runs made, and why it was only half true

Every sweep since #69 has recorded "no server / listener — already covered by `no-network-client`, which bans `import Network` outright." That reasoning holds for a Network-framework listener and nothing else. A listener does not have to come through the Network framework:

- `socket(2)` is reachable from plain `import Foundation` (Darwin is re-exported on macOS)
- `NSXPCListener`, `CFSocket*` and `NSSocketPort` are Foundation types
- an embedded HTTP server (Vapor, SwiftNIO, Swifter, GCDWebServer, Telegraph…) arrives as a package import, not as `import Network`

Checked rather than argued: a file whose only content is `let fd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0)` passes `check_the_world.mjs` on `main` today. With the new rule registered it produces exactly one finding, from `no-listener` — `no-network-client` stays silent, which is the gap. This is the genuinely new angle the prior "already covered" note was missing.

### The false alarm the check is shaped around

A bare `listen(` is **deliberately not banned**. LaughCounter's entire domain vocabulary is listening — `requestListening()`, `finishListening()`, `private var listening`, `keepMacAwakeWhileListening` — so a mic-listening method named `listen()` would be a false alarm the day someone wrote it. Dropping it costs nothing: a BSD socket is created before it is listened on, so `socket(` catches the same code one line earlier, and "socket" carries no microphone meaning in this repo. A fixture pins the vocabulary as a non-finding. Same discipline as `no-audio-persistence` excluding `AVAudioFile(forReading:)`.

### Deletion test — the paragraph went whole

Unlike the three prior conversions, whose paragraphs each kept judgment the check couldn't hold (what a new persisted field *means*; extending the directory vs earning a second one), this paragraph had nothing left over once the check was authored to carry it:

- the rule → the check
- "a decision about exposing the laugh log, not a feature to slip in" → the finding's `why`
- "the owner's explicit sign-off, a loopback-only default, and a story for authentication or CSRF" → the finding's `fix`, stated there rather than in `description` (a finding renders `what`/`why`/`fix`/`doc`, never `description`)
- the history — a web dashboard once existed in the Python reference and was removed on purpose → the module's header comment, where the skill puts rationale

So it was deleted whole rather than trimmed. It's the one judgment call in the PR and it's flagged there for the owner; reverting one hunk restores it. `README.md`'s enforcement table moves the "No server / listener" row from prose to the check.

### Left as prose, re-verified this run

- **"There is no accepted egress — none"** — held by `no-network-client`. (Its coverage does have thinner edges too — `Data(contentsOf:)` against a remote URL, `NSURLSession` which `\bURLSession\b` doesn't match — but `Data(contentsOf: fileURL)` is exactly how `Store.swift` reads the laugh log, so a check there would fire on the real tree. ## What converted

**`laughcounter`: "Don't prune a `.gitignore` section in the same breath as deleting what it ignored" → `laughcounter/no-committed-artifacts`** (blocking).

The paragraph describes an accident with a static signature: a build artifact sitting in the repo's file set. No `ctx.read` needed — the path is the whole signal.

It fires *earlier* than the prose's own story does. `ctx.files` is tracked files plus untracked files git does **not** ignore, so the artifacts enter the file set the instant their ignore rule is deleted, while they are still sitting untracked in the worktree — before any commit exists. What is enumerable is the other side: the artifact shapes, taken from this repo's own `.gitignore` plus the toolchains this tree has hosted (SwiftPM/Xcode, the Python reference, macOS packaging, Node).

1	# Working in this repo
2	
3	The general lessons this repo has paid for once. The privacy boundary — the
4	product's defining constraint — has its own pack (`local/on-device-privacy`);
5	what follows is everything else.
6	
7	**Don't prune a `.gitignore` section in the same breath as deleting what it
8	ignored — the artifacts are still on disk.** Removing a toolchain (the Python
9	reference, a build system, a generator) invites tidying its ignore rules away in
10	the same commit, but the ignored artifacts it already produced are usually still
11	sitting untracked in the worktree — earlier test runs leave `__pycache__/`,
12	builds leave `build/`. The moment those rules go, the next `git add -A` sweeps
13	the artifacts *into* the very commit that was supposed to remove them, and
14	nothing complains: the commit is valid, the tests still pass, and the junk only
15	shows up as an inflated file count in the diff a reviewer reads. Delete the
16	artifacts from the worktree first (or `git clean` them), then drop their ignore
17	lines — and read `git diff --cached --stat` after any bulk `git add -A`, not just
18	`git status`, since staged additions are exactly what a clean `git status` stops
19	telling you about.
20	
21	**"Not statically checkable" is a verdict about the tree's shape at the time, not
22	about the rule — re-ask it after the tree changes.** `on-device-privacy`'s
23	"everything lives in one deletable directory" sat as prose because proving it
24	looked like it needed data-flow tracking of a `FileManager` write target back to
25	its declaration — true while the Python reference had many entry points, and
26	false the moment that tree went away: the native app has exactly two persistent
27	path roots, both the same search-path lookup, so constraining the *root*
28	constrains every path derived from it and no tracing is needed. A removal, a
29	migration, or a consolidation can collapse the entry points a rule has to cover,
30	so when a sweep meets prose a previous sweep left behind, re-derive the objection

# On-device privacy — the boundary the whole product is built around

An always-on microphone in someone's living room only earns its place if what it
hears stays on the machine. That promise is the product requirement
(`docs/DESIGN-AND-TRADEOFFS.md` §0/§6, README *Privacy*), the text of the mic and
speech prompts users actually see (`mac/Resources/Info.plist`), and the reason
several design choices look heavier than they need to. The checks in this pack
hold the mechanical half; what follows is the judgment half.

There is now exactly one implementation — the native app in `mac/Sources/` — so
every rule below is about it.

**What may cross the boundary: derived metadata, never audio.** A laugh is
persisted as time, duration, confidence, and an origin label — that is what the
JSONL lines carry, and `LaughStore` says so in its own header. **No audio is
stored at all** — the `no-audio-persistence` check holds this mechanically for
v1. A feature that wants to keep audio (the v3 roadmap's rolling buffer) changes
the mic prompt and this check together, in the same PR.

**Everything lives in one deletable directory.**
`~/Library/Application Support/LaughCounter/` holds the laugh log and the app's
own diagnostic log — the `single-storage-directory` check holds this mechanically,
by allowing `.applicationSupportDirectory` and nothing else as a search-path root.
The one path macOS dictates, not us, is a Login Item registration, which names no
directory of its own.

**There is no accepted egress — none.** Detection (Sound Analysis) and speech
recognition (`SFSpeechRecognizer` with on-device recognition required) are both
built into macOS; no model is downloaded, no telemetry is sent, and the app makes
no outbound connection of any kind. The `no-network-client` check is therefore
absolute rather than carve-out-shaped. Adding *any* egress — a model fetch, a
crash reporter, a sync feature — is a product decision that gets written here and
in the README *Privacy* section before a line of it is written in Swift.

`NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` and `NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription` tell
the user audio is analysed on-device and not recorded.

The executor carries **no schedule of its own**: give it a cron and it silently becomes a second orchestrator with a competing trigger. One schedule, owned by the orchestrating routine; executors run only when dispatched. State only the executor's *contract* in the routine's prose (what it computes, what the agent may rely on) — its internal rules live in its code, unlike validators of the agent's *own* output, which the prose must still teach (see the routine-folder rules below).

Symptoms you've absorbed what belongs elsewhere: the spec re-explains a companion script's logic or a sibling doc's steps, or has grown to several times its sibling routines (the house norm is ~40–90 lines).
14	- Bound an unattended agent's **write surface**, and enforce it from outside the agent. A setup-phase failure that reports itself but leaves the original trigger untouched (e.g. a label still set) makes the item look unprocessed rather than blocked, silently defeating the escalation path. Treat every failure mode as equivalent from the triage perspective.
16	- An unattended agent must **never invoke a tool that surfaces a blocking approval it cannot answer** — there is no human present to click "Allow," so the run stalls indefinitely on step one. Push that boundary continually: each time a step proves mechanical, move it out of the prompt and into the workflow.

The executor carries **no schedule of its own**: give it a cron and it silently becomes a second orchestrator with a competing trigger. One schedule, owned by the orchestrating routine; executors run only when dispatched. State only the executor's *contract* in the routine's prose (what it computes, what the agent may rely on) — its internal rules live in its code, unlike validators of the agent's *own* output, which the prose must still teach (see the routine-folder rules below).

Assert the expected shape in the first lines and throw with a message naming the missing field. (A harness gotcha in the same family: pass structured args as actual JSON values, not a JSON-encoded string — a stringified object reaches the script as one string and every field access yields `undefined`; a fan-out panel once reviewed "undefined" in place of the proposal it was convened on, flagged only by the agents themselves.)
- **When a task needs several deferred/lazily-loaded tools (schemas fetched via a tool-search or discovery call rather than present from the start), load them all in one batched query up front, not one per turn.** The full set of tools a flow will need is usually knowable before the first call; fetching each one's schema separately as the need arises costs a round trip per tool for no added information.
- **In an agent config file (e.g. `CLAUDE.md`), `@import` only docs whose guidance applies to essentially every session; point at a specialized or pipeline-specific doc with a plain link instead.** An `@import` is expanded inline at launch in *every* session regardless of relevance, taxing the always-loaded context budget; a plain link is read on demand only when its trigger fires. Reserve `@import` for baseline, always-relevant practice, and route a self-contained pipeline/release/maintenance doc through a soft pointer instead.
- **A SessionStart hook gates work through the session context it injects, not by blocking.** The hook's stdout becomes context the agent reads — the runtime never intercepts it — so enforcement is the agent's instruction-following, not the hook itself. Use it for setup/environment validation: output a STOP directive on failure (the agent asks the user before proceeding); emit nothing on success.
- **For an open-ended visual/layout requirement, render real candidate designs and let the owner pick before building one.** When the spec leaves *how it looks or groups* open, drive the production renderer with hand-shaped fake data and put 2–4 *actually-rendered* options in front of the owner, rather than fully implementing, testing, and snapshot-approving a single interpretation that a later reorientation then discards wholesale. Reach for throwaway mockups through the real render path at the first sign of layout ambiguity — *ahead* of the implement→test→snapshot-approve cycle, which only kicks in once a change already exists.
- **When asked to *show* or *see* a visual artifact, deliver the image into the chat — not a path or a link.** Surface the file itself so it renders inline; a link or bare path makes the owner go fetch it. For a tiny artifact (e.g. a 16/32px icon) also include an exact nearest-neighbor upscale, labelled as enlarged, so the detail stays legible.
- **When a routine regenerates a reviewable artifact (a gallery, a snapshot set, a report), surface it in the chat the same turn you commit it** — a URL to the branch's copy, or the file rendered inline — so review is one click away instead of a hunt. (Complements the show/see rule above: that's for an artifact the owner asked to *see*; this is for one a routine *regenerates*.)
- **When driving a CI-gated merge via API/MCP poll rather than the shell, merge on an already-green required check — don't trigger or wait for a duplicate run.** A push already ran CI on the head commit; opening a PR on the same commit fires an identical second run that adds no signal. If the check isn't yet green, poll on a rolling backoff (e.g. 5 s → 10 s → 15 s → 30 s) until it settles; never tight-poll; and don't subscribe for green — CI success transitions are frequently not delivered as webhook events, so the green signal never arrives.
- **When an action you take kicks off an async downstream process whose output matters to what happens next (a merge triggering a build/publish/deploy), don't report the task done until that process completes and its output exists — poll for it.** Reporting at the trigger point races the async process: a follow-up action taken right after (e.g. "now ship this") would then operate on the stale prior output instead of the one just triggered.
- **In a multi-stage agent pipeline, every failure exit must converge to the same human-triage state.** A setup-phase failure (page download, authentication, scaffolding) that posts a comment but leaves the original trigger label in place makes the item look unprocessed rather than blocked, defeating the escalation mechanism. Treat every failure mode — pre-agent setup, agent bail, post-agent quality check — as equivalent from the triage perspective: all must resolve to the same visible state (e.g. a comment naming what failed, plus the trigger label removed).

3	// invokes every active pack's `session-end.mjs`; this one runs the same capture the

5	//
6	// WHY it earns its place: capture at merge time sees only MERGING sessions, and only
7	// up to the merge. This event captures the sessions that never merge — a review, an

10	//
11	// It can double-write with a merge capture, and that is safe by construction, not by
12	// coordination: capture keys its delta on the SESSION ID across every prior file for
13	// that session, so a second event for a session pushes only the entries after the
14	// first, and a zero delta pushes nothing at all (capture-log.mjs, pinned by tests).
15	//
16	// Best effort. Nothing depends on this having run — every firing enriches the
17	// record, every miss leaves exactly the merge-only behaviour. The runner swallows a
18	// non-zero exit, so this reports honestly rather than pretending to succeed: a repo
19	// with no `origin` remote, or no transcript on disk, simply exits non-zero and the
20	// runner logs it.
21	import { spawnSync } from 'node:child_process';
22	import { dirname, join } from 'node:path';
23	import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';
24	
25	const capture = join(dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)), 'capture-log.mjs');
26	
27	// The engine runner hands on what the harness told it about this session; capture's
28	// own discovery (CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID, then the newest transcript) is the fallback
29	// when the hook ran without input.
30	const transcript = process.env.CLAUDINITE_TRANSCRIPT;
31	const session = process.env.CLAUDINITE_SESSION_ID;
32	
33	// The issue this session was ABOUT, when its launcher knew one — the runner's
34	// documented pass-through (engine/hooks/session-end-command.mjs). A hook firing
35	// carries none and captures as issue 0; the scheduler's executor session runs the
36	// runner explicitly at the end of its dispatch and names that dispatch issue, so an
37	// unattended run's log is filed under the task it ran instead of vanishing into the
38	// issueless pile. Anything that is not a non-negative integer is ignored rather than
39	// passed on — capture's argument validation is not the place to discover a typo.
40	const raw = process.env.CLAUDINITE_SESSION_ISSUE ?? '';
41	const issue = /^\d+$/.test(raw.trim()) ? raw.trim() : '0';
42
